name: Third-wave feminism
summary: Third-wave feminism, a 1990s current led by Generation X women after the Anita Hill hearings, joins gender with race, class and sexuality (intersectionality) and treats gender as constructed and the category of women as unfixed. It is sex-positive, plays with femininity, welcomes queer and trans people, and favours personal narrative, cultural critique and direct grassroots action over a single programme. Its own writers say it has no unified agenda, so it states few positions on economics, government or foreign affairs.
scope: The English-language, mainly American third wave from Rebecca Walker's 1992 'Becoming the Third Wave' on: Britannica's account, Snyder's scholarly reading, and the Manifesta authors' own account, with riot grrrl and Walker's Third Wave Direct Action Corporation (named by Britannica) as parts the defining sources name. It leaves out second-wave radical, socialist and anti-pornography feminism, the theorists (Butler, Crenshaw) as authorities in their own right beyond what the defining sources attribute to the movement, and later fourth-wave online feminism.

missingStatements.text: Women should be free to express their sexuality as they choose without being judged or shamed for it.
missingStatements.rationale: Snyder reports that third-wavers claim sexual pleasure as they desire it and refuse to judge others' sexual choices.
missingStatements.declined: Mostly a matter of social attitude rather than law; legalize-sex-work and restrict-private-adult-pornography-access already place the ideology on sexual freedom.

missingStatements.text: Racism, sexism and class oppression overlap and cannot be addressed one at a time.
missingStatements.rationale: Britannica names intersectionality (race, gender, class and sexuality interacting) a key concept of the third wave, and Snyder says its core move is an intersectional version of feminism.

missingStatements.text: Transgender and non-binary people should be fully included in the legal and social category of women or gender-based protections.
missingStatements.rationale: Snyder reports that third-wave thinking, with its gender continuum and antiessentialism, fits transgender people more fully than second-wave thinking did.

notes: The American Prospect piece (s3) names the movement only as 'the third wave', so no current answer rests on it. Pass 2 (2026-11-17) rebuilt the answers on Britannica, Snyder (Signs 2008), the Manifesta authors' interview, The American Prospect, the National Women's History Museum and the Walker biography (not cited). Answers that rested only on Wikipedia or on a general value were nulled. Themes searched with no stated position found: economy and markets, taxation and welfare, property, public ownership, government structure and elections, courts, executive power, federalism, war and military, foreign policy, immigration and citizenship, religion and law, environment and technology, crime and punishment, speech and censorship. Third-wave sources stress multivocality and decline a unified agenda (Britannica; Snyder), so the record on these themes is silent. Crenshaw's article (s2) and the Wikipedia pages (s1, s4) stay listed because earlier history entries cite them, but no current answer rests on them.
